method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: Democrats won both the US Senate and the House in Tuesday's midterm elections, and the dollar fell to a one-month low as US yields dropped on bets a split government borrows less; US stocks rallied about 2%. Strong job openings and a healthy services survey still keep a December Federal Reserve rate rise likely, so Friday's jobs report decides whether the slide lasts.

EUR.text: The euro rose to about $1.125 as the dollar slid on the Democratic sweep of the US Congress. Euro-zone inflation rose to 4.0% in October as expected, driven by energy, which keeps a December European Central Bank rate rise possible without adding urgency; the race to replace ECB President Christine Lagarde is the main unknown.

GBP.text: The pound climbed to its highest since mid-September as the dollar fell on the US midterm results, and economists expect the Bank of England to raise its rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since 2023. Most of the gain came from a weaker dollar, so the Bank's vote split and guidance decide whether it holds.

JPY.text: The yen firmed slightly to about 158.3 per dollar as US yields fell on Democratic midterm gains and Tokyo stocks dropped 3%, which usually sends money toward the yen. The Bank of Japan has signalled a likely December rate rise, but the dollar still sits near the 160 area where Tokyo has stepped in before.

CHF.text: Swiss inflation jumped to 1.5% in October on dearer fuel, above forecasts, which makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to justify. The franc also gains when investors look for shelter, and while Iran peace talks sap that demand, US strikes on an Iranian island and a deadly attack on a ship off Oman show the fighting has not stopped.

CAD.text: Oil, Canada's main export, fell about 8% on Wednesday as markets bet the Iran war winds down, which weighs on the Canadian dollar. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem has said more rate rises may be needed with inflation near 3%, but cheaper oil weakens both the trade support and some of the inflation case.

AUD.text: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, but Governor Michele Bullock said it is time to take stock, which reads as a pause. China's services growth slowed to a three-month low and Asian stocks fell on the US midterm results, both of which weigh on the Australian dollar, though a weaker US dollar softens the hit.

NZD.text: New Zealand's jobless rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest since 2015, which makes further Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate cuts more likely. Slower services growth in China, its biggest customer, adds to the pressure, while a third straight rise in global dairy prices is the main support.

XAU.text: Gold climbed back above $4,000 an ounce, up about 2%, as the dollar fell to a one-month low and US yields eased after Democrats won both houses of Congress; central banks also bought 42% more gold last quarter. Markets still expect a December Federal Reserve rate rise, so Friday's US jobs report decides whether the rebound holds.

OIL.text: Brent crude plunged about 8% to near $95 a barrel, its lowest in almost two months, as traders bet that Democratic control of Congress and Vice President JD Vance's comment that the war cost his party the election push Washington toward ending the Iran war. Peace talks through Qatar and Pakistan continue, but a single new strike or attack on Gulf shipping could reverse the drop.

items.headline: Oil plunges about 8%, Brent near $95, as markets bet the Iran war winds down
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 8.5% to near $95 a barrel and US crude dropped below $89, the lowest in almost two months, as traders bet that Democratic control of Congress pushes Washington toward ending the war with Iran.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has kept oil above $100 for weeks by choking tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the main exit for Gulf oil. Democrats won both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, and many voters blamed the war for high fuel prices.
beats.happened: Brent fell 8.5% to $94.83 and US crude (WTI) fell 7.5% to $88.88 in Wednesday's US session, more than 15% lower over the week. Peace talks through Qatar and Pakistan have resumed, though Iran's leadership said anyone expecting a US policy shift after the vote is mistaken.
beats.means: A large part of the war premium is coming out of the price on the view that the new Congress will limit funding for the war. Gulf exports had already been recovering, so supply looks less tight. Any new strike or attack on shipping could reverse much of the drop quickly.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil hurts the Canadian dollar, since oil is Canada's main export, and helps big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone. It also eases the inflation worry behind the Federal Reserve's expected December rate rise.

impact.why: The biggest one-day fall in months as bets grow that the war ends.
Much lower prices for Canada's main export.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a smaller import bill helps the yen.

items.watch: Any new US strike or attack on Gulf shipping, and whether the US-Iran talks set a next meeting.

items.headline: Vice President Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US Vice President JD Vance said voter anger over the Iran war was the main reason Republicans lost both houses of Congress, and backed calls for a diplomatic end to the fighting.

beats.was: The US has been at war with Iran for months, and fuel prices have soared. Democrats won control of the Senate and the House in Tuesday's midterm elections.
beats.happened: In his first comments since the results, Vance wrote on X that the war was the reason his party lost, and called a diplomatic resolution sensible. He led US negotiators in spring talks whose deal later collapsed. President Trump said the war will end when he decides it ends.
beats.means: A senior figure in the administration openly blaming the war adds to the sense that Washington wants a way out, which helped drive Wednesday's oil slide. It is a signal, not a policy change: Trump still controls the decision.
beats.fx: Talk of ending the war lowers oil prices and cuts demand for safe havens like the Swiss franc and gold.

impact.why: A top official backing diplomacy raises the odds the war ends.
Less need for a safe place to park money if the war winds down.

items.watch: Whether the White House changes its Iran stance, and the next round of talks through Qatar and Pakistan.

items.headline: US stocks head for their best day in three months after the midterms
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: US shares jumped about 2%, with the Dow up more than 1,500 points by midday, and US 10-year borrowing costs fell to 4.90% as investors welcomed the end of one-party control in Washington.

beats.was: Democrats won both houses of Congress on Tuesday, ending Republican control of Washington. Asian stocks fell overnight on worries about tighter rules for AI firms.
beats.happened: By midday in New York the S&P 500 was up 1.8% and the Dow 2.9%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell from 4.95% to 4.90%, as investors expect a split government to add less debt. Oil companies and defense firms fell as oil dropped below $95.
beats.means: Wall Street read the result as calmer, not riskier: less new borrowing, and a better chance the Iran war ends. That reverses much of the overnight fear in Asia.
beats.fx: Lower US yields take away some of the dollar's appeal, and a strong mood in markets usually favors riskier currencies like the Australian dollar over safe havens.

impact.why: Lower US yields and less need for safety.
A strong mood in global stocks tends to lift the Australian dollar.

items.watch: The US jobs report on Friday, November 6, and whether stocks hold their gains into the close.

items.headline: US crude stocks fall only slightly, far less than an industry survey suggested
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Official US government figures showed crude oil stocks fell by about 0.9 million barrels last week, a much smaller drop than the 5.3 million barrel fall an industry survey reported on Tuesday.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, keeping oil above $100 a barrel. Weekly US stock figures show how tight supply is; Tuesday's industry survey from the American Petroleum Institute hinted at a big drawdown.
beats.happened: The Energy Information Administration, the US government's energy statistics agency, said commercial crude stocks fell about 0.9 million barrels in the week to October 30.
beats.means: US supply looks less tight than Tuesday's survey implied, which takes a little support away from prices. Talks between Washington and Tehran still matter far more than one week of stock data.
beats.fx: A small weight on oil is a small weight on the Canadian dollar, since oil is Canada's main export.

impact.why: A smaller fall in stocks than the industry survey pointed to.
Slightly less support for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Any news on US-Iran talks or new attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: US services growth eases a little in October, slightly below forecasts
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The Institute for Supply Management's survey of US service firms slipped to 54.5 in October from 54.9, just under the 54.8 expected, but hiring improved and every part of the survey still showed growth.

beats.was: Services are most of the US economy. Strong figures this week, including a jump in job openings, have kept markets expecting the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December to fight inflation.
beats.happened: The survey read 54.5 (above 50 means growth). New orders and business activity slowed, while the hiring gauge rose to 51.4 and the prices firms pay stayed very high at 73. The survey said many firms have not yet passed tariff and fuel costs on to customers.
beats.means: Services are still growing at a healthy pace and price pressure is not fading, so this does little to weaken the case for a December Fed rate rise. The dollar barely moved.
beats.fx: A neutral print for the dollar: it neither adds to nor reverses today's slide after the midterm results.

impact.why: Slightly softer growth, but firmer hiring and high prices keep a December Fed rise on the table.

items.watch: The US jobs report on Friday, November 6, the last big test before the Fed's December decision.

items.headline: Oil turns lower, Brent near $101, as a Democratic Congress may limit US action on Iran
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude gave up an early gain and fell about 2% to near $101.65 a barrel, as traders weighed whether a Democratic Congress will hold back new US military action against Iran.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has pushed oil above $100 a barrel by disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil. Prices fell 7% on Monday when Iran signalled it was open to peace talks.
beats.happened: Brent fell 1.9% to $101.65 and US crude (WTI) fell 1.9% to $94.33 in a swinging session. Analysts said Democratic control of both houses of Congress could restrict President Trump's foreign policy, including money for military operations abroad. Qatar said its mediation between Washington and Tehran goes on, with no breakthrough yet.
beats.means: Some of the war-risk premium is leaving the price as new US strikes look less likely. But Neil Shearing, chief economist at Capital Economics, warned that renewed strikes could lift Brent above $120, so prices can still swing hard.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil weighs on the Canadian dollar, since oil is Canada's main export, and eases price pressure for big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Less chance of new US strikes takes some war premium out of the price.
Lower prices for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Official US oil stock figures at 9:30 a.m. CT today, and any sign of new US strikes or a deal with Iran.

items.headline: Euro-zone inflation rises to 4.0% in October, as expected
items.story_title: ECB: a December rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: Prices in the 20 countries that use the euro rose 4.0% over the past year in October, up from 3.8%, matching forecasts. Energy did most of the lifting.

beats.was: Energy costs have climbed since the Iran war disrupted Gulf oil and gas, pushing euro-zone inflation to about double the European Central Bank's 2% goal. The ECB has signalled it could raise rates in December.
beats.happened: Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, said in its first estimate that inflation rose to 4.0% in October, as economists expected. Inflation without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco held at 2.5%, also as expected, while energy prices were about 21% higher than a year ago.
beats.means: The rise comes from energy, not from broader price pressure, since the underlying measure did not move. That keeps a December ECB rate rise possible but adds no new urgency.
beats.fx: No surprise, so little fresh push for the euro either way; the euro's gains today come from the weaker dollar.

impact.why: In line with forecasts: higher inflation backs a possible rate rise, but steady underlying prices add no urgency.

items.watch: The ECB decision on December 17, and whether energy prices keep rising.

items.headline: Gold climbs back above $4,000 as the dollar and US yields fall after the midterms
items.story_title: Gold: Fed rate-rise bets vs a weaker dollar
items.summary: Gold rose about 2% and crossed back above $4,000 an ounce as the dollar fell to a one-month low after Democrats won both houses of the US Congress.

beats.was: Gold slid in October to about $3,870 last Friday, near its lowest in a year, as markets came to expect a December rate rise from the US Federal Reserve. Higher rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
beats.happened: December gold futures traded near $4,027 early Wednesday, up 2.2% from Tuesday, and spot gold crossed $4,000, after Democrats won the House and the Senate. The dollar index fell to about 101.5, Treasury yields dropped, and silver jumped about 4%.
beats.means: A split government is expected to borrow less, which keeps US yields lower and helps gold. Markets still put the chance of a December Fed rate rise near 78%, so the bounce depends on the dollar staying weak.
beats.fx: A weaker dollar and lower yields lift gold; this is a rebound, and the Fed headwind has not gone away.

impact.why: Back above $4,000 as the dollar and US yields fall.
Gold's jump mirrors the dollar's slide to a one-month low.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report for October, which will shape December Fed rate-rise bets.

items.headline: Democrats take control of the US Senate after winning key midterm races
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: Democrats won back the US Senate on Tuesday night, taking Republican seats from Iowa to Texas. With the House also going their way, President Trump faces a Congress run by the other party.

beats.was: Before Tuesday's midterm elections, President Trump's Republicans held both the Senate and the House, which let them pass tax cuts and spending with little resistance. Democrats needed to gain four Senate seats, which looked hard.
beats.happened: The Associated Press reported that Democrats retook the Senate, winning Republican-held or open seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa. US networks had already projected a Democratic House, and the AP called the House for Democrats early Wednesday.
beats.means: A Democratic Congress can block new tax cuts and big spending plans for the rest of Mr Trump's term, so the US is likely to borrow less than it would have. Less borrowing points to lower US bond yields over time.
beats.fx: Lower expected yields take some support from the dollar, which slipped to a one-month low in Asian trading as the results came in.

impact.why: A Congress controlled by Democrats means less new borrowing and lower yields, which weighs on the dollar.
Lower US yields make gold, which pays no interest, a little more appealing.
The euro rose to about $1.125 as the dollar fell on the results.

items.watch: Whether US bond yields keep falling, and whether Friday's US jobs report keeps a December Federal Reserve rate rise likely.

items.headline: Democrats projected to win control of the US House of Representatives
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: US networks projected late Tuesday that Democrats will take the House from President Trump's Republicans; the Senate is still too close to call.

beats.was: Americans voted on Tuesday in the midterm elections, which decide all 435 House seats and 35 of 100 Senate seats. Republicans held both chambers, which let President Trump pass tax cuts and spending with little resistance.
beats.happened: Major US networks projected just before 10 p.m. Eastern that Democrats will win a House majority. In the Senate, Democrat Roy Cooper took a Republican seat in North Carolina, but control was still open, and a 50-50 split would leave Republicans in charge through Vice President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote.
beats.means: A Democratic House can block new tax cuts and big spending plans from next year, which points to less government borrowing and lower US bond yields. Much of this was expected, so the Senate result now decides how big the shift is.
beats.fx: Lower expected yields weigh on the dollar; a Democratic Senate as well would add to that pressure.

impact.why: A split government means less borrowing and lower yields, which takes some support from the dollar.
Lower US yields make gold, which pays no interest, a little more attractive.

items.watch: Whether Democrats also win the Senate, and whether the Associated Press confirms the House call.

items.headline: Japan's Nikkei drops 3% as Democratic gains in the US midterms hit AI stocks
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: Tokyo's main share index fell about 3% on Wednesday, led by chip and AI names, on worry that a Democratic Congress will tighten rules on data centres.

beats.was: Japanese shares had climbed to records this year on the boom in artificial-intelligence spending, with chip and cable makers among the biggest winners.
beats.happened: The Nikkei 225 fell 3.1% to about 61,128 early Wednesday. SoftBank Group lost about 7%, memory maker Kioxia 10% and chip-testing firm Advantest 6.4%, as investors bet Democrats would bring tighter rules on data-centre projects.
beats.means: A sharp fall in stocks tends to send money toward safe assets, and the yen usually benefits when Japanese investors pull back from risk.
beats.fx: Mild support for the yen through risk aversion, against the much bigger pull of the gap between US and Japanese interest rates.

impact.why: Falling stocks tend to send money into the yen as a safe place.
The Australian dollar tends to slip when Asian stocks sell off.

items.watch: Whether the sell-off spreads to US stocks when New York opens on Wednesday.

items.headline: Stocks and the dollar slide after early Democratic wins in the US midterms
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The dollar fell about 0.3% and US bond yields dropped as early midterm results favoured the Democrats, lifting the euro and pound.

beats.was: The dollar had firmed earlier on Tuesday after strong US job-openings and factory figures, which raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.
beats.happened: As Democrats won key Senate races in Georgia and North Carolina, the dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, fell 0.3% to about 101.4. The 10-year US Treasury yield dropped about 6 basis points to 4.91%, the euro rose 0.4% to about $1.124 and the pound 0.4% to about $1.346.
beats.means: Traders read Democratic gains as a check on government borrowing, which lowers the yields that have been pulling money into the dollar.
beats.fx: The euro and pound gain most directly from a softer dollar; how far it goes depends on the Senate count.

impact.why: Falling Treasury yields on Democratic gains pulled the dollar lower across the board.
The euro rose to about $1.124 as the dollar weakened.
The pound rose to about $1.346 ahead of Thursday's expected Bank of England rate rise.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report, which could restore the dollar's support if it is strong.

items.headline: Oil edges lower as investors wait for US midterm results
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude slipped to about $103.30 a barrel early Wednesday, near a four-week low, as traders weighed the US election and a stalled US-Iran peace effort.

beats.was: Oil has swung with every turn in efforts to end the war between the US and Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent fell to its lowest in nearly four weeks on Tuesday.
beats.happened: Brent fell about a quarter of a percent in Asian trading and US crude dipped to about $95.60. A senior Iranian official said the two sides are still far from a deal, while President Trump said the US has no immediate plans to strike Iran. An industry survey showed US crude stocks fell by about 5.3 million barrels last week, against expectations of a small rise.
beats.means: Prices are drifting while there is no clear news on peace talks. Falling US stockpiles give some support underneath, and official US government stock figures are due Wednesday.
beats.fx: Slightly cheaper oil is a mild drag on the Canadian dollar and eases inflation worries for oil importers such as Japan.

impact.why: No progress either way on Iran left prices drifting lower.
Oil is Canada's biggest export, so softer prices weigh a little on its currency.

items.watch: Official US crude stock figures on Wednesday, and any news from the US-Iran talks.

items.headline: China's services growth slows to a three-month low in October
items.story_title: China: a slowing economy
items.summary: China's private services survey fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6, still growing but at the slowest pace in three months.

beats.was: China's private factory survey beat forecasts on Monday, but the wider economy has been uneven, with firms cutting prices to win customers.
beats.happened: The RatingDog China services PMI, a business survey where 50 separates growth from shrinking, fell to 50.8 from 51.6. Companies kept cutting prices while their costs, including oil and wages, rose at the fastest pace in five months, and their confidence dropped to a three-month low. The combined factory and services reading eased to 52.0 from 52.4.
beats.means: China's economy is still growing, but firms are squeezed between rising costs and price wars, which caps how much they buy from abroad.
beats.fx: A small drag on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, whose exports depend on Chinese demand.

impact.why: Slower Chinese services growth hints at softer demand for Australian exports.
China is New Zealand's biggest buyer, so slower growth there weighs on the kiwi.

items.watch: China's October trade figures, due later this week.

items.headline: Dollar falls to a one-month low as Democratic wins raise worries about tighter AI rules
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The dollar index slipped to about 101.4, a one-month low, as investors worried a Democratic Congress could tighten rules on artificial intelligence, the spending that has driven much of US growth.

beats.was: US growth this year has leaned heavily on company spending on AI and data centres. Strong US data had markets expecting a December Federal Reserve rate rise, which supported the dollar.
beats.happened: After Democrats won the House and the Senate on Tuesday, the dollar index fell to 101.41. The euro rose 0.4% to $1.1236, the pound rose 0.46% to $1.3475, a seven-week high, and the dollar slipped to 158.09 yen and 0.8162 Swiss francs. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.92%.
beats.means: Investors fear tougher AI rules could slow growth and lessen the need for Fed rate rises. Strategists at Convera and OCBC bank noted that passing laws stays hard while President Trump holds a veto, so yields and economic data matter more than politics for the dollar.
beats.fx: Mild pressure on the dollar against every major currency; a Commonwealth Bank of Australia strategist said a sharp rise in oil is the main thing that would lift it again.

impact.why: Worries that tighter AI rules slow US growth and the need for rate rises.
Pound at a seven-week high as the dollar slips.
Euro at its highest in nearly two weeks.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report for October, and whether AI-linked US stocks keep falling.

items.headline: Gold edges up as cheaper oil eases inflation worries before US election results
items.story_title: Gold: Fed rate-rise bets vs a weaker dollar
items.summary: Gold rose 0.2% to about $3,935 an ounce early Wednesday in Asia, helped by oil's slide to a four-week low.

beats.was: Gold fell to its lowest in a year last Friday, below $3,900, as Federal Reserve officials talked up more US rate rises, which make an asset that pays no interest less attractive.
beats.happened: Spot gold rose 0.2% to about $3,935 in early Asian trade after oil fell to its lowest in nearly four weeks on Tuesday. Markets still put about a 78% chance on a US rate rise in December, and the World Gold Council expects India's gold buying this year to drop to a six-year low because of high prices.
beats.means: Cheaper oil cools the inflation worry behind expected rate rises, which gives gold some room, but strong odds of a December Fed rise and weaker Indian demand keep pressure on it.
beats.fx: A small bounce rather than a turn: gold stays near its yearly low until rate-rise bets fade.

impact.why: Cheaper oil eases inflation worries, but a likely December Fed rise limits the bounce.

items.watch: Whether the US jobs report on Friday changes the odds of a December Fed rate rise.

items.headline: Pound climbs to its highest since mid-September as the dollar slides
items.story_title: Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023
items.summary: The pound rose above $1.345 in Asian trading on Wednesday, its highest since September 16, as the dollar fell on the US midterm results and markets wait for a Bank of England rate rise on Thursday.

beats.was: The pound has been helped by expectations that the Bank of England will raise its rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since 2023, because energy costs are pushing UK inflation up.
beats.happened: Sterling rose past the middle of the $1.34s, a seven-week high, as the dollar index fell to its lowest in over a month on Democratic wins in the US midterms. Easing worries about UK public finances after recent budget updates also helped.
beats.means: Most of the move came from a weaker dollar rather than news from Britain, so Thursday's Bank of England vote and guidance decide whether the pound can hold its gains.
beats.fx: Pressure is upward for the pound and downward for the dollar; a cautious Bank of England could take some of the gain back.

impact.why: A weaker dollar and an expected Bank of England rate rise lift the pound.
The dollar's slide on the midterm results drove most of the move.

items.watch: The Bank of England's vote split and guidance on Thursday, November 5.

items.headline: Central banks bought 42% more gold in the third quarter, the World Gold Council says
items.story_title: Gold: Fed rate-rise bets vs a weaker dollar
items.summary: Central banks bought about 320 tonnes of gold from July to September, 42% more than a year earlier, even as high prices cut jewellery buying to a record low for the quarter.

beats.was: Gold has fallen to near its lowest in a year as markets bet on a December rate rise by the US Federal Reserve, since higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
beats.happened: The World Gold Council, the gold industry's research body, said central banks stepped up purchases in the third quarter, and gold funds took in about 210 tonnes. Jewellery demand fell 17% and coin and bar buying fell 19% as prices averaged about $4,260 an ounce. Total demand was roughly flat.
beats.means: Steady buying by central banks puts a floor under demand even when households pull back. It is backward-looking, though, and does not change the near-term pull from US interest rates.
beats.fx: Mild support for gold; the bigger driver remains Fed rate expectations.

impact.why: Strong central-bank buying supports demand, though it covers last quarter, not this week.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report and what it does to the odds of a December Fed rate rise.

items.headline: New Zealand's jobless rate rises to 5.7%, its highest since 2015
items.story_title: New Zealand: a weakening jobs market
items.summary: New Zealand's unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the July–September quarter, worse than the 5.5% expected, and the number of people in work fell.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand kept its rate at 2.75% on October 28 when many expected a rise, saying it wanted to see how its two earlier increases were working. It still said more rises were likely.
beats.happened: Statistics New Zealand said unemployment rose to 5.7% from 5.6%, the highest in about ten years, against forecasts of 5.5%. Jobs fell 0.1% in the quarter when a 0.4% gain was expected, fewer people were looking for work, and private-sector pay growth slowed to 2.0% over the year.
beats.means: A softer jobs market and slower pay growth make it less likely prices keep rising fast, which supports the central bank's decision to wait and weakens the case for another rate rise soon.
beats.fx: Less chance of higher New Zealand rates takes support from the kiwi, which slipped toward 55.9 US cents after the release as two-year interest-rate bets fell.

impact.why: A clear jobs miss lowers the odds of another New Zealand rate rise.
Weak news next door adds to the soft mood for the Australian dollar after its own central bank hinted at a pause.

items.watch: Whether New Zealand's central bank drops its hint of more rate rises at its next decision.

items.headline: US crude stocks fell 5.3 million barrels last week, an industry survey shows
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: The American Petroleum Institute's weekly survey showed US crude stocks fell by about 5.3 million barrels, a much bigger drop than the week before.

beats.was: With Gulf supply cut by the Iran war, analysts watch US stockpiles for signs of how tight the market is. Analysts had expected a small rise last week, which would have been the first in five weeks.
beats.happened: The American Petroleum Institute, an industry group, said crude stocks fell 5.27 million barrels in the week to October 30, after a 2.0 million barrel fall the week before. The government's official figures follow on Wednesday.
beats.means: A fifth straight weekly fall, if the government numbers confirm it, says US demand and exports are still drawing down reserves even as peace hopes pull prices lower.
beats.fx: Falling stockpiles put a small floor under oil prices, a mild help for oil-linked currencies such as the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: A bigger-than-expected stock drop points to a tight US market, pending official figures.
Firmer oil gives Canada's currency slight support.

items.watch: The US Energy Information Administration's official stock figures on Wednesday morning.

items.headline: Dollar edges up after strong US data, pushing the yen toward 158.5 per dollar
items.story_title: Japan: guarding the yen near 160 per dollar
items.summary: The dollar gained a little on Tuesday after US job openings and factory orders beat forecasts and US bond yields rose, and the yen weakened toward 158.5 per dollar.

beats.was: The yen fell to about 160 per dollar earlier this year, a level where Japan's government has stepped in before to buy yen. Since then Tokyo has repeated that it will act against wild moves, and the Bank of Japan has hinted at a rate rise in December.
beats.happened: US job openings rose to about 7.5 million in September and factory orders grew 1.8%, both above forecasts. US two-year bond yields rose above 4.6% and ten-year yields above 4.9%, and the dollar climbed toward 158.5 yen, a level it has failed to break several times.
beats.means: Firm US data supports the Federal Reserve officials who want another rate rise in December, which keeps the interest gap between the US and Japan wide. That gap is the main reason the yen stays weak.
beats.fx: Higher US yields help the dollar most against the yen; the closer it gets to 160, the more likely Japan's warnings turn into action, which caps how far the move can go.

impact.why: Rising US yields widen the gap with Japan's low rates and push the yen weaker.
Two data beats and higher bond yields give the dollar a small lift before the midterm results.

items.watch: Whether the dollar breaks above 158.5 yen, and any new warning from Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama.

items.headline: Global dairy prices rise 3% at the latest auction, a third gain in a row
items.story_title: New Zealand: dairy prices and the kiwi
items.summary: Prices at the Global Dairy Trade auction, where New Zealand's Fonterra and others sell milk products, rose 3% on Tuesday, more than expected and the third rise in a row.

beats.was: Dairy is New Zealand's biggest export, so prices at the twice-monthly Global Dairy Trade auction feed straight into farm incomes and demand for the New Zealand dollar. The kiwi has been weak since New Zealand's central bank skipped an expected rate rise on October 28.
beats.happened: The auction's price index rose 3.0%, after a 2.5% gain at the previous sale, with an average price of about $4,166 a tonne. Forecasters had expected no change, and 111 buyers won at least one bid.
beats.means: Three firm auctions in a row point to steady overseas demand for New Zealand's main product, which helps farm incomes and the country's trade balance.
beats.fx: Better dairy prices give the kiwi mild support, but on their own they rarely outweigh interest rates, and New Zealand's central bank has stepped back from raising them.

impact.why: Higher prices for New Zealand's biggest export lift its trade income.

items.watch: New Zealand's third-quarter jobs figures, out this evening US time.

items.headline: US factory orders rise 1.8% in September, beating forecasts
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: Orders placed with US factories rose 1.8% in September, more than the 1.2% economists expected, led by aircraft and spending tied to artificial intelligence.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its main rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on October 28, but two governors wanted a rise, and markets lean toward a December hike. Monday's survey of purchasing managers showed US factory output booming in October.
beats.happened: The Commerce Department's monthly count of new factory orders rose 1.8%, and August was revised up. Aircraft orders jumped about 28%. Orders for business equipment outside aircraft and defence, a guide to company investment plans, rose 0.6%.
beats.means: Firms are still spending, especially on computers and data centres for artificial intelligence, so the economy is not slowing much. Economists warn that higher rates and squeezed household budgets could cool factories next year.
beats.fx: Solid spending gives the dollar a little support, since it adds to the case for another Fed rate rise. It lands after a strong job-openings report, so the two point the same way.

impact.why: Strong orders add a little to the case for a December Fed rate rise.

items.watch: Friday's US October jobs report.

items.headline: US job openings jump to 7.52 million in September, and more people quit
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: US employers had about 7.52 million unfilled jobs at the end of September, well above the roughly 7.1 million economists expected, while layoffs fell and more workers quit to move on.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its main rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on October 28, but two governors voted for a rise, and markets have leaned toward a December hike. The JOLTS survey, the US Labor Department's monthly count of job openings, hires, quits and layoffs, is one of the last checks on hiring before Friday's October jobs report.
beats.happened: Openings rose by about 333,000 to 7.52 million, and August was revised up to about 7.2 million. Quits, people leaving a job by choice, rose to about 3.37 million, a sign workers feel they can find another one. Layoffs fell to about 1.64 million.
beats.means: Firms still want workers and few are cutting staff, so pay pressure is unlikely to fade fast. That supports the Fed officials who want one more rate rise to cool inflation. The survey gets fewer replies than it used to, so one month can be noisy.
beats.fx: A firmer job market gives the dollar some support, because it makes a December rate rise easier to justify. The bigger tests are tonight's midterm results and Friday's jobs report.

impact.why: More openings and fewer layoffs back the case for a December Fed rate rise.

items.watch: Friday's US October jobs report, which shows whether the hiring signal holds up.

items.headline: Iran says it shot down a US drone over Hormuz as Yemen's Houthis push toward a second oil sea lane
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they downed a US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen's Houthi rebels have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia while moving toward the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

beats.was: The US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, and Iran's hold on the Strait of Hormuz has choked much of the Gulf's oil exports. Qatar and others are mediating a draft deal, but a senior Iranian official said on Tuesday the two sides are still far apart.
beats.happened: After US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island overnight, which a US official called defensive, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they shot down an American MQ-9 drone over the eastern end of the strait. Reuters also reported that the Houthis, Iran-backed rebels in Yemen, have hit Saudi oil sites and Riyadh's airport and are advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow strait at the mouth of the Red Sea.
beats.means: Fighting around the talks has not stopped. A Houthi threat to the Bab el-Mandeb matters because Saudi Arabia has been sending more of its oil out through the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz.
beats.fx: More risk to Gulf and Red Sea shipping props up oil, which helps Canada's dollar and hurts big oil buyers like Japan; markets mostly looked past it on Tuesday as hopes for a deal held.

impact.why: A threat to the Red Sea route adds a second supply worry, though prices still eased on deal hopes.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so wider shipping risk raises its energy bill.

items.watch: Any Houthi attack on ships near the Bab el-Mandeb, and whether Washington answers Iran's latest proposal.

items.headline: Race to replace Lagarde at the ECB begins, with nominations due Friday
items.story_title: ECB: choosing Lagarde's successor
items.summary: Euro-zone governments have until Friday, November 6, to name candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde as European Central Bank president; Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot lead early betting.

beats.was: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, said on October 29 she will leave on February 7, about nine months before her term ends. The same day the bank held its deposit rate at 2.5%.
beats.happened: Euro-zone finance ministers will review nominations on November 9, and a winner needs the backing of at least 16 of the 21 member countries. Front-runners are Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements and former Bank of Spain governor, and Klaas Knot, who ran the Dutch central bank for 14 years. Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel also leaves in January and chief economist Philip Lane's term ends in May, so half the bank's top board changes within five months.
beats.means: The next president will shape euro-zone rates for eight years. Knot has a record of favouring tighter policy, while Hernández de Cos is seen as more middle-of-the-road, so the choice could shift how quickly the bank raises or cuts in future. Lagarde still chairs the December and February meetings.
beats.fx: Little effect on the euro for now, since nothing changes before February, but a clear lean toward a tougher-on-inflation pick would give the euro mild support.

impact.why: A leadership change ahead, with the direction of policy depending on who wins.

items.watch: Which names governments submit by Friday, November 6, and what the finance ministers signal on November 9.

items.headline: Pound holds near $1.344 as banks expect the Bank of England to raise rates on Thursday
items.story_title: Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023
items.summary: The pound sat near $1.344 on Tuesday as economists expect the Bank of England to lift its rate to 4% on Thursday, with ING forecasting a 7-2 vote.

beats.was: The Bank of England has kept its rate at 3.75%, but the jump in energy costs from the Iran war has pushed UK inflation up. It has not raised rates since 2023.
beats.happened: ING economists James Smith and Michiel Tukker expect a quarter-point rise to 4% on Thursday, November 5, with seven of nine policymakers voting for it. They note markets already expect more than a full percentage point of rises in total, and the pound held near $1.344.
beats.means: A rise is close to certain, so the vote split and what the Bank says about further rises matter more than the decision. A message that more rises are likely would back what markets already expect.
beats.fx: The pound has been helped by the view that high energy costs leave the Bank little choice; firm guidance would support it, while a wide split or a softer tone could knock it.

impact.why: A rate rise is widely expected and mostly priced; the vote and guidance decide the move.

items.watch: The Bank of England decision and vote on Thursday, November 5.

items.headline: Oil climbs back as Iran says a peace deal is still far off
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil rose almost 2% on Tuesday, with Brent near $106.60 a barrel, after a senior Iranian official said Tehran and Washington are far from a deal to end their war.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for about eight months, and Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the Gulf's oil, has kept prices high. On Monday oil fell more than 7% on hopes that talks hosted by Qatar would end the fighting.
beats.happened: A US official confirmed American forces struck Iran's Qeshm Island, inside the strait, calling it a defensive move to stop attacks on merchant ships. A senior Iranian official then said the two sides are far apart and Tehran will not accept what it sees as too much being asked of it, though parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Iran had sent its reply and now waits on Washington. Brent rose about $1.80 and US crude about $1.60, to near $98.
beats.means: Monday's hope that the war is ending has cooled a little, so some of the extra price for war risk is back in oil. Talks have not collapsed, which keeps a lid on the bounce for now.
beats.fx: Dearer oil helps the Canadian and Norwegian currencies and hurts big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone; it also nudges up inflation fears, which tends to support the dollar.

impact.why: Iran says a deal is far off, putting some war risk back into prices after Monday's big fall.
Oil is Canada's main export, so a rebound gives the loonie a little help.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dearer oil weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Washington answers Iran's reply, and any new attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: Indian cargo ship hit off Oman; one sailor killed
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: An Indian-flagged cargo ship was hit by an unidentified flying object off Oman on Monday, killing one of its 14 crew; it adds to a string of attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: Ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, have come under repeated attack during the Iran war, including tankers hit over the weekend. Oil had just fallen sharply on hopes of peace talks.
beats.happened: India's shipping minister, Sarbananda Sonowal, said the cargo vessel AL JUSUFI was struck near the coast of Oman on November 2. One sailor died and the other 13 were rescued by Oman's coast guard. No one has said who carried out the attack.
beats.means: It was a small cargo ship, not an oil tanker, so supply is not directly hit. But a deadly attack shows the waters around Hormuz are still dangerous even as talks go on, which keeps shipping and insurance costs high.
beats.fx: Adds a little support to oil and to currencies of oil exporters, and a touch of shelter demand; small on its own.

impact.why: Another attack near Hormuz keeps supply worries alive, though no oil cargo was hit.

items.watch: Whether attacks on ships keep coming while US-Iran talks continue.

items.headline: Australia's Bullock says it is time to take stock after the rate rise; Aussie dips below 70 US cents
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said after Tuesday's rate rise that it is a good moment to pause and check the data, and the Australian dollar slipped below 70 US cents.

beats.was: Earlier on Tuesday the Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate by a quarter point to 4.85%, its fifth rise of 2026, in a six-to-three vote with three board members wanting to hold.
beats.happened: At her press conference, Governor Bullock said she does not know what the next move will be, but it is probably a good point to take stock and see whether the data match the bank's forecasts. She said the three who wanted to hold worried more about housing and rising unemployment, and that the bank is not aiming for a recession. The Australian dollar fell about 0.3% to near 69.8 US cents, around a two-week low.
beats.means: Together with the split vote, this reads as a pause after a long run of rises, though she kept the door open because inflation risks still point up. A December rise now looks less likely than before the meeting.
beats.fx: Leans on the Australian dollar, since markets see fewer rate rises ahead than they did a day ago.

impact.why: A clear hint of a pause, and the currency dropped below 70 US cents.
The kiwi tends to follow the Australian dollar.

items.watch: Australian jobs and inflation data before the December 8 meeting.

items.headline: Reserve Bank of Australia raises rates to 4.85%, as widely expected
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth rise this year, but three of its nine board members wanted to hold and it gave no hint of more.

beats.was: Australian prices have kept rising fast this year, helped by fuel costs from the Iran war, and the central bank had already lifted its rate four times in 2026. Markets put the chance of another rise at close to 90%, so the move itself was no surprise.
beats.happened: The board lifted the cash rate by a quarter point to 4.85%, its highest since 2008. The vote was six to three, with three members preferring to stay at 4.60%. New forecasts show inflation above 3% for the next year and only reaching the top of the 2-3% target by late 2027, while unemployment rises more than expected. The bank said it will watch the data rather than promising further rises.
beats.means: A split board and no signal of more rises suggest this could be the last increase for now, even though inflation is expected to stay too high for longer. Governor Michele Bullock's press conference is the next clue on whether a December rise is still on the table.
beats.fx: The higher rate was already priced, so the Australian dollar gets little new lift from it; the three dissents and the open-ended wording lean against a lasting gain.

impact.why: A higher rate supports it, but the 6-3 split and no hint of more rises cut the case for further gains.
The kiwi often moves with the Australian dollar, so a cautious hike gives it little help.

items.watch: Governor Michele Bullock's press conference on whether more rises are possible, and the December 8 decision.

items.headline: China's PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD
items.story_title: China: slowing the yuan's climb
items.summary: China's central bank will make banks hold more of their foreign-currency deposits in reserve from November 15, a step aimed at slowing the yuan's rise.

beats.was: The yuan has gained more than 5% against the dollar this year, one of Asia's best runs, and sits near a four-year high. The People's Bank of China had already been setting its daily reference rate weaker than expected, a sign it wanted the climb to slow.
beats.happened: The bank said banks must hold 6% of foreign-currency deposits in reserve, up from 4%, starting November 15. That takes dollars out of China's banking system, making them a bit scarcer and so less cheap to buy with yuan. It reverses a cut made in 2023, when Beijing was fighting a falling yuan.
beats.means: Beijing is telling markets it does not want the yuan to rise too fast, since a strong currency hurts its exporters while the economy is slowing. The direct effect on money flows is modest; the message matters more.
beats.fx: A slower-rising yuan tends to drag a little on currencies that trade as stand-ins for China, chiefly the Australian and New Zealand dollars.

impact.why: The Australian dollar often tracks the yuan, so Beijing leaning against yuan gains weighs on it.
China is New Zealand's biggest buyer, so a capped yuan gives the kiwi less support.

items.watch: Whether the yuan's daily reference rate keeps coming in weaker than expected after the change takes effect on November 15.

items.headline: Iran offers to reopen Hormuz within two days if the US meets its terms
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's foreign ministry said it could restore safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz within two days, down from a seven-day plan, if Washington accepts its demands.

beats.was: Iran has restricted the Strait of Hormuz, the main route for Gulf oil, since the war with the US and Israel began in February. In September Tehran set out a seven-day plan to reopen it, tied to ending the war, lifting oil sanctions and freeing its frozen money.
beats.happened: Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Iran had cut that timetable to two days as a sign of good faith, as long as its demands are met. President Masoud Pezeshkian said the Supreme Leader has given the government room to negotiate, while Iran's navy said another tanker caught fire after hitting mines near the strait.
beats.means: It is the clearest sign yet of how fast oil could flow again if a deal is struck. But the conditions are the same ones Washington has resisted, and the Wall Street Journal reported the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, heavy strike campaign after the midterms.
beats.fx: A quick reopening would pull oil down sharply, helping Japan and the euro zone and weighing on Canada's dollar; for now it is an offer, not a deal.

impact.why: Shows supply could return within days of a deal, but the offer comes with terms the US has not accepted.

items.watch: Whether the US responds to Iran's terms, and whether any tankers cross Hormuz without being hit.

items.headline: Oil ends near a four-week low as hopes grow for talks on both the Iran and Ukraine wars
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude closed about 1% lower on Tuesday at $103.60 a barrel, its lowest close since early October, as traders bet on talks to end the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

beats.was: Iran has blocked most tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key Gulf shipping lane, during an eight-month war with the US, which pushed oil well above $100. Prices fell 7% on Monday on signs of peace talks.
beats.happened: Brent, the global benchmark, settled at $103.60 and US crude at $96.09, both their lowest closes in several weeks. Russia said it will hold three-way talks with Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, and Qatar, which is carrying messages between Washington and Tehran, said both sides are still reviewing proposals, even though an Iranian official says a deal is far off.
beats.means: Two separate peace tracks give the market reasons to expect more supply later, but nothing is agreed and fighting goes on, so prices are falling slowly rather than collapsing.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil eases pressure on big energy buyers such as Japan and the euro zone, while it takes some support from oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Peace-talk hopes on two fronts pull prices to multi-week lows.
Lower oil prices trim Canada's export income.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so cheaper oil helps its trade balance.

items.watch: The US-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, and any word from Qatar on a US-Iran proposal.

items.headline: Oil gives back its morning bounce and falls for a second day on peace-talk hopes
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil turned lower in US trading on Tuesday, with Brent near $103 a barrel and US crude near $95, as hopes for US-Iran peace talks outweighed overnight US strikes on an Iranian island.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran keeps most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil, shut. Oil fell about 7% on Monday on hopes of a peace deal, then rose almost 2% early Tuesday after US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island.
beats.happened: By midday in New York the early rise had gone. Brent slipped about 1% to near $103 and US crude to near $95, a second daily fall, as traders bet the talks will carry on despite the strikes.
beats.means: The market is treating the Qeshm strikes as a one-off rather than a return to full fighting, and is pricing a better chance of a deal. Prices are still far above where they started the year, so any setback can quickly undo the drop.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil helps big energy buyers like Japan and the euro zone and eases inflation worries, while it takes some support from the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Hopes for a peace deal win out over the overnight strikes, pulling prices down a second day.
Oil is Canada's main export, so a lower price trims support for the loonie.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so cheaper oil eases the drain on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Washington replies to Iran's latest proposal, and whether Iran answers the Qeshm strikes.

items.headline: Bank of Canada's Macklem tells MPs further rate rises could be needed
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: a rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem told a parliamentary committee the bank may need to raise rates again but will move carefully, repeating last week's message.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on October 28, its first rise since 2023, to stop high fuel prices from spreading into wider inflation. Canada's inflation has run near 3% since April.
beats.happened: Speaking to the House of Commons finance committee, Macklem said inflation could reach about 3.5% by year-end and stay at or above 3% through much of 2027. Further rises are possible, he said, but the bank will decide one meeting at a time.
beats.means: Nothing new: he repeated last week's guidance almost word for word. Markets see roughly even odds of another rise at the December 9 meeting.
beats.fx: The message keeps some rate support under the Canadian dollar, but since it was already expected, it adds little. Oil, Canada's main export, still matters more day to day.

impact.why: Keeps a December Bank of Canada rate rise possible, though already expected.

items.watch: Macklem speaks to a Senate committee on Thursday, November 5; the next rate decision is December 9.

items.headline: Strategists still see a weaker dollar ahead, but more now fear it holds up
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: A Reuters poll of currency strategists still sees the euro climbing to about $1.16 within a year, but most of those asked think the dollar is more likely to beat their forecasts than fall short.

beats.was: The dollar has slipped to near a one-month low, with the euro around $1.12, as oil fell on hopes of an end to the Iran war. Americans vote on Tuesday in midterm elections that decide control of Congress.
beats.happened: Reuters' monthly poll of 66 forecasters put the euro at about $1.13 in three months and about $1.16 in a year, so the call for a weaker dollar stands. But 17 of 30 strategists asked a follow-up question said the dollar is more likely to come in stronger than they forecast.
beats.means: Forecasters keep their view of a slowly weaker dollar, but they are less sure of it, with US growth holding up and the Federal Reserve leaning toward another rate rise rather than cuts.
beats.fx: The poll adds little new pressure on its own. It shows the expected path for the dollar is lower, but the risks around that path tilt toward a firmer dollar.

impact.why: Forecasts still point lower, but most strategists asked see more risk of a stronger dollar.
The median forecast has the euro rising toward $1.16 over the next year.

items.watch: Midterm results overnight and Friday's US jobs report, which will show whether the dollar steadies.

items.headline: Swiss inflation jumps to 1.5% in October on fuel costs
items.story_title: Switzerland: inflation picks up on fuel costs
items.summary: Swiss prices rose 1.5% from a year earlier in October, up from 1.0% and above the 1.3% expected, almost entirely because fuel got dearer; underlying prices stayed calm.

beats.was: Swiss inflation has been very low for two years, inside the Swiss National Bank's 0-2% target, and some traders had hoped the bank would cut its rate again in December. The Iran war has pushed fuel prices sharply higher this year.
beats.happened: The Federal Statistical Office said prices rose 0.2% in the month, against no change expected, and 1.5% over the year, the highest since late 2023. Petrol, diesel and heating oil drove nearly all of it. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and fresh food, held at just 0.5%.
beats.means: Higher headline inflation makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to argue for. But because the rise is in fuel and not in everyday prices, the bank is unlikely to feel pushed to raise rates.
beats.fx: Supports the Swiss franc by cutting the odds of a December rate cut; the calm core reading limits how far that goes.

impact.why: A clear beat that makes a December rate cut less likely.

items.watch: The Swiss National Bank's December 10 decision, and whether fuel costs keep rising.

items.headline: US carries out 'defensive' strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, officials say
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US officials said American forces made limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, hours after President Trump played down new attacks; oil edged back up in Asia.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran keeps most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, shut. Oil fell about 7% on Monday on hopes for a peace deal after Trump said he was not planning strikes after the US midterm elections.
beats.happened: The Wall Street Journal first reported, and a US official then confirmed, strikes on Qeshm, the biggest island in the strait. Officials called them limited and defensive, a reply to Iran firing missiles at US aircraft, and said they do not mean full fighting has restarted. Iranian state media reported several blasts on the island. Brent crude rose about 0.5% to near $105 a barrel in early Asian trade.
beats.means: Even with talks moving and both sides sounding hopeful, the two militaries are still trading fire around the strait. That keeps a risk of escalation alive and makes the market's bet on a quick deal shakier.
beats.fx: Any sign the fighting is not over adds some war premium back to oil and supports the dollar and Swiss franc as safe places to hold money, while it hurts big energy buyers like Japan.

impact.why: Fresh US-Iran fire in the strait revives the risk to Gulf supply after Monday's big drop.
Renewed war risk adds some demand for the dollar as shelter.
Investors lean on the franc when conflict risk rises.
Japan imports almost all its energy, so pricier oil weighs on it.
Canada exports oil, so a firmer oil price helps its currency.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the Qeshm strikes, and whether the draft deal from the Qatar talks survives them.

items.headline: Trump raises doubts about renewed attacks on Iran
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Asked on Monday whether he was weighing new strikes on Iran after Tuesday's US midterm elections, President Trump said no, and Vice President JD Vance said talks with Iran have gone well.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran has kept most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, shut. Trump had hinted for days that strikes could resume once the midterm vote was over, which kept a risk of fresh fighting hanging over markets.
beats.happened: After a speech in Washington he billed as his closing pitch before the vote, Trump answered no when reporters asked about post-election strikes, and said he thinks Iran wants a deal and one could happen. Vance said there had been several good conversations with the Iranians and that he and Trump feel hopeful about a negotiated end. Trump repeated that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.
beats.means: This is the clearest sign yet that the feared post-election strike window may not come, coming a day after Iran's leadership backed the talks. Nothing is agreed, though: Iran still wants the US blockade of its ports lifted first, and attacks on Gulf shipping have not stopped.
beats.fx: Less chance of new strikes takes some war premium out of oil and trims demand for the dollar and the Swiss franc as safe places to hold money, while it helps big energy buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Ruling out post-election strikes lowers the risk of a new hit to Gulf supply.
Lower war risk trims demand for the dollar as a safe place.
Calmer markets reduce the pull of the franc as shelter.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so a softer oil price helps it.
Canada exports a lot of oil, so a lower oil price weighs on its currency.

items.watch: Whether Washington formally answers the draft deal circulating in Qatar, and whether Iran gets any move on the port blockade.
